scenes.sub: Moving through memory one element at a time.
scenes.say: Pointer arithmetic. Adding to a pointer doesn't add bytes. It moves by whole elements. Let's walk through an array.

scenes.head: p + 2 means two ints, not two bytes

panels.code:
int arr[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
int* p = arr;        // &arr[0]
int* q = p + 2;      // &arr[2]

std::cout << *q;     // 30
std::cout << q - p;  // 2

p++;                 // now &arr[1]

scenes.say: p starts at the first element, address hex one hundred. p plus two doesn't add two bytes. It adds two times the size of an int, eight bytes, so q points at the third element. Dereferencing q gives thirty. Subtracting pointers gives the distance in elements, so q minus p is two, not eight. And p plus plus steps to the next int, four bytes along.

scenes.head: The step size comes from the type
scenes.say: The step size comes from the pointer's type. An int pointer moves four bytes per step, a double pointer moves eight, on typical platforms. That's also why standard C plus plus forbids arithmetic on a void pointer: there's no size to step by. And here's the secret: a of two is defined as star of a plus two. Array subscripting is pointer arithmetic.

scenes.head: Where it's legal
scenes.say: The rules. You may point anywhere inside the array, or exactly one past the end. One past the end is legal to hold and compare, but never to dereference. Going any further, even without dereferencing, is undefined behavior. Subtracting pointers into different objects is also undefined. Used correctly, this is exactly how iterators work: loop from the start until you reach end.

lines: p + n moves n elements, i.e. n × sizeof(T) bytes.
q − p is the distance in elements; a[i] is *(a + i).
Valid only inside one array, or one past its end. Anything else: UB.
scenes.say: Adding n to a pointer moves n elements, which is n times the size of the type in bytes. Subtracting two pointers gives the distance in elements, and a of i is just star of a plus i. It's only valid inside one array, or one past its end. Anything else is undefined behavior.
